To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) Students who attend a two-week, non-academic computer science outreach program can learn a substantial amount of computer science content, including concepts such as event-driven programming, message passing, initialization of state and say/sound.

(1) our students learned computer science concepts, and (2) our students learned the concepts of event-driven programming, state initialization, message passing, sound/say synchronization, and conditional branching.

(1) a two-week, non-academic, interdisciplinary summer camp can be an effective means of imparting CS concepts to middle school students; (2) students can learn event-driven programming, state initialization, message passing, sound and say synchronization in a two-week camp; and (3) we have employed assessment methodologies in the form of a series of tasks that can be used to assess student knowledge of CS concepts in the context of outreach programs.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how we can best teach computer science to students who may not have access to a formal computer science education.
the design of a curriculum and an assessment methodology that can be applied to other outreach programs.
the learning of middle school students in a Scratch-based outreach program.

it is possible to design and implement assessment methodologies that allow for the assessment of computer science concepts, even in the absence of a traditional classroom setting.
a two-week summer camp can be used not only to engage students in CS, but also to teach CS concepts.
